speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) whether the Ministry tracks data on the overall recycling rate by region and globally; (b) if so, whether the Ministry has observed a declining trend in the overall recycling rate regionally and globally; and (c) how does Singapore’s overall recycling rate compare with other countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for
text: Sustainability and the Environment): Mr Speaker, may I have your permission to answer oral Question Nos 15 to 18 on today’s Order Paper?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A breakdown by the type of the amounts of waste generated, disposed of and recycled can be found on the National Environment Agency (NEA) website.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, even if recycling is technically possible, it may not always be practical or economical to do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are several economic, logistical and behavioural factors determining our recycling rates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, the business case for recycling has deteriorated due to rising logistics, freight, manpower and energy costs across the wider landscape.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These rising costs make it less viable for recyclers to operate a sustainable business around collecting and recycling of material.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Second, export markets for recyclables have become increasingly stringent in their requirements.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Singapore exports most of its recyclables for further processing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Tightening export requirements by the receiving countries could limit the quantity our local recyclers can sell.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And third, the contamination of recyclables remains a persistent challenge, limiting the volume of recyclables that can be recovered and processed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These three challenges make the situation complex and contribute to the lower recycling rates we have seen in recent years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The definitions of recycling rates also vary internationally, with no consensus on the definitions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some countries report recycling rates across different waste streams, others use a broader definition of what counts as recycled, such as including energy recovery or repurposing of waste residues within their national recycling rate, which we do not.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Comparing recycling rates across countries is therefore not always meaningful if the bases are different.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, we do believe that we can and must do more to strengthen resource circularity in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is why I had earlier announced that the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) and NEA will be reviewing the 2019 Zero Waste Masterplan to strengthen our approach to waste management.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While we are striving to achieve these targets, we will review them for relevance given the changing waste and recycling landscape.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the targets to be meaningful, we will address the challenges associated with recycling of both domestic and non-domestic waste.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are studying how we can increase the yield of clean, segregated recyclables that are easier for recyclers to meet regulatory requirements.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will engage the waste generators to explore better ways to segregate waste upstream in the processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For households, the blue bin network under the National Recycling Programme remains the primary channel for recycling.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, blue bins are managed by our Public Waste Collectors (PWCs), who are required to provide one blue bin per HDB block and clear recyclables up to three times a week.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To address higher recycling demand and overflowing bins in certain areas, PWCs have deployed additional bins at around 700 locations and increased the collection frequency at more than 1,100 locations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: NEA and the Town Councils (TCs) also conduct joint site inspections to address estate-specific issues, such as bin placement and damaged bins, with straightforward issues typically resolved within two days.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Efforts introduced by the PWCs include implementing smart recycling bins, door-to-door collection services, Cash-for-Trash events,+--*- or partnering TCs to set up metal cages or points for bulk collection.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Five TCs have come forward to partner the PWCs in dedicated collection, and we have seen encouraging results in collecting paper and cardboard with lower contamination rates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We encourage all TCs and community stakeholders to reach out and partner with their PWCs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have also introduced source-segregated recycling at the national level, such as via the Return Right – Beverage Container Return Scheme.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: By nudging consumers to make a small change in their lifestyle, we hope to increase the recycling of beverage containers and spark a change in our recycling habits.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Moving forward, we will explore more ways to enhance the National Recycling Programme to reduce contamination and improve the volume of clean recyclables recovered from households, building on ground-up recycling initiatives.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This could include the use of source-segregated bins.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Recycling is important, but we must also reinforce the other "2Rs" – Reducing waste at the outset and Reusing where possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have seen some encouraging progress on this front.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will explore how we can better support efforts to shape consumption patterns and the growth of more sustainable business models.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Another strategy that we are embarking on is the strengthening of the reuse of waste residue and treated toxic industrial waste before and after they are landfilled.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The recently launched Towards Resource Efficiency And Sustainability for URban EnvironmentS (TREASURES) Centre will focus on building the technologies and the risk assessment frameworks for this purpose.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The first one, will NEA consider adjusting gate fees for industrial and commercial waste collection to shift behaviour of businesses towards higher recycling rates, especially for food waste which accounts for about 11% of total waste but has a very low recycling rate of only 18%?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: My second supplementary question pertains to the blue bins.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned there is a high contamination rate, which renders the recycled or collected items non-recyclable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Will there be any plans for NEA to consider a national recycling campaign to reduce blue bin waste contamination?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The incentives and disincentives around recycling and waste disposal are an important part of it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will consider her suggestion on looking at the fees.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue of blue bin contamination continues to be something that we have to engage in terms of public education and shifting behaviours.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It will certainly form an important part of the review of the Zero Waste Masterplan.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Beyond recycling rates, can the Ministry consider complementary indicators and targets such as waste reduction, material circularity or recycling contamination rates to better measure progress towards a circular economy?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The second supplementary question will be: how will the Ministry assess whether public education campaigns are working, translating into sustained improvements in recycling behaviour rather than short-term participation?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, the issue of how we should think about recycling and waste disposal will be at the heart of our review of our Zero Waste Masterplan.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue that she brought up in her first supplementary question: should we focus purely on the recycling rate?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The reality is, today, we look at all of these things.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The study and the review will address whether we should introduce new indicators or whether we should change the emphasis between the indicators that we currently track, measure and target.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: She is right to then highlight that public education campaigns should look at what the outcomes are.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not only look at, for example, participation in public education campaigns or awareness.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do track the waste production recycling rates and many other outcome indicators, and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: What are the measures MSE will take to help Singaporeans realise this?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We can draw reference from the European Union's (EU's) Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation that minimises the amount of packaging generated.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Or even radio-frequency identification (RFID)-based food waste sorting systems.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: My second supplementary question: businesses can be required to accept reusable containers, supplying repairable products or refills.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: What are the policy thresholds that MSE considers to disincentivise single-use packaging or restrict aggressive promotional tactics which may put more products into the market?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think this is a marker of the awareness from the various campaigns and the engagement that Singaporeans have with the importance of this issue.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It gives us the foundation to think about how we might take the next steps in terms of our Zero Waste Masterplan and achieve the very important outcomes around reducing waste that is diverted towards Semakau Landfill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We actually have a number of pilots, studies and stakeholders that are looking at many of these measures.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are looking for tools and mechanisms to improve the outcomes, to reduce the amount of waste that we generate and to increase the recycling of the ways that we do generate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What we have to do is to keep our focus on the outcomes – whether it is about mechanisms such as packaging regulation, technologies such as RFID or the policy thresholds for disincentives.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have to look at the outcomes in terms of waste generation and recycling rates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In some cases, some of these tools may end up diverting behaviour to an alternative waste stream and alternative packaging, which potentially may be harder to recycle or may have other consequences for the environment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we do have to look at it holistically, whether it is about a policy threshold for a disincentive, technology implementation or regulation that we impose on businesses, what is the outcome around waste generated.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just one supplementary question on whether there are any recycling plans in the pipeline for collaborations with our partners in the region or globally, or for a start, coming up with a common framework in terms of recycling across our Association of Southeast Asian Nations region?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are business arrangements between businesses here in Singapore and businesses in the region or overseas, to be able to handle the recycling of waste and recycling of material, whether domestic or non-domestic, already today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Those arrangements allow for businesses to address a larger market, potentially reap economies of scale and become sustainable as a commercial interest, which gives us the opportunity to then have the capacity to further recycle.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to work with stakeholders and partners on making sure that this is a viable process.
